title: PhaseFold: Sequence-aware kernel orchestration with quantized fallback and prefill prioritization
creator: Aisha Patel
description: PhaseFold is an orchestrator that combines a lightweight sequence-length predictor, a compact cost/latency model, and a constrained online tuner to pick the most efficient kernel for each request class. The goal is to reduce steady-state token cost and overall GPU time by selecting quantized kernels where safe, while preserving p95/p99 latency SLOs. It prioritizes prefill routing decisions (prefill-first vs decode-first kernels), manages a small probe budget for cold kernels, and supports fast rollback to conservative kernels when tail latency degrades.
acceptance_criteria: Integrated PhaseFold decision path into runtime request router with feature flag behind 'phasefold-opt-in'
End-to-end canary shows >=8% reduction in mean GPU-seconds per token for mixed webchat workload without >5% p99 latency regression
Fallback/rollback path triggers within 10s when p99 exceeds threshold and returns to last-good kernel
Probe budget enforced (max 10 probes/min per worker) and probe outcomes logged to kernel telemetry
Perf dashboard panels for PhaseFold decisions, probes, and rollback events added to runtime-console
tasks: Design: define sequence-length buckets, feature vector set (seqlen, model-arch, prefix-hit-rate, quantized-compatibility)
Prototype: implement lightweight predictor (XGBoost-lite) in C++ runtime shim with feature extractor
Cost model: build parametric model mapping kernel variant -> (median latency, p99 delta, tokens/sec, GPU-seconds/token)
Tuner: implement constrained multi-armed bandit with probe budget and exponential backoff for risky kernels
Routing: wire PhaseFold into prefill/decode decision path with telemetry hooks
Canary: rollout plan, traffic slicing, and alerting (auto-rollback on SLA breach)
Dashboard and logs: add metrics, traces, and sampling to Console; create dashboard link
Docs: update runtime docs and engineering runbook for incident response and tuning knobs

decisions: Use a small deterministic model (XGBoost-lite / one-tree forest) for on-worker prediction to avoid RPC calls and cold latency
Keep probe budget conservative (10 probes/min/worker) and enforce a per-kernel cooldown window to reduce oscillation
Favor latency-safe kernels for p99-critical customers by applying a penalty term in the cost model rather than a hard veto
Quantized kernels allowed as fallbacks only if historical quality regression < 0.5% on eval prompts and decode path has >=95% functional parity checks
tradeoffs: Using an on-worker predictor increases binary size marginally but avoids RPC/coordination; chosen for tail latency stability
Conservative probe budget reduces exploration and may delay cost wins on new kernels, but minimizes user-visible regressions
Penalty-based approach for p99 allows more cost savings than a strict safe-only policy, but requires careful penalty calibration
